# Introduction

This exercise utilizes the [suburban Cook County Health Atlas](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org) and [Chicago Health Atlas](https://chicagohealthatlas.org) indicators to evaluate select public health outcomes relative to transportation access and quality across Cook County. The exercise will make use of indicators derived from local surveys (i.e., [Cook County Health Survey](https://cookcountypublichealth.org/health-survey/) and the [Healthy Chicago Survey](https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/cdph/supp_info/healthy-communities/healthy-chicago-survey.html)) that are administered annually by the two local health departments. Both surveys are designed to collect neighborhood-level information from residents on such things as health status, risk behaviors, and access to health care to inform and monitor the health status of communities. [Download the exercise #4 presentation](slides/Exercise04_Template.pptx) template to organize data elements and summaries. Submit the completed presentation to the appropriate submission folder on D2L.

# Step 2. Create health and transportation indicator dataset

## Combine countywide geographies

Use the following code to create a novel geography (N=202) that combines city of Chicago community areas (N=77) and suburban Cook County municipalities (N=125 using 4 square mile threshold area) using GEOJSON data imported from the two health atlases.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false

# import City of Chicago community areas (N=77) GEOJSON and transform to local projection for spatial analysis (epsg:3435)

community_areas <- st_read("https://metopio.blob.core.windows.net/lalage/atlas/3/shapes/communityareas.topo.json", quiet=TRUE) %>% 
  st_as_sf() %>% 
  st_set_crs(4326) %>% 
  st_transform(3435) %>% 
  rename(geoid = id) %>% 
  mutate(geoid= str_replace(geoid,"1714000-",""),
         location = "Chicago, IL",
         type = "community area")

# import places within suburban Cook County (N=125) and transform to local projection for spatial analysis (epsg:3435)

places_cook_county <- st_read("https://metopio.blob.core.windows.net/lalage/atlas/6/shapes/SCC-place.topo.json", quiet=TRUE) %>% 
  st_as_sf() %>% 
  st_set_crs(4326) %>% 
  st_transform(3435) %>% 
  rename(geoid = id) %>% 
  mutate(sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) * 0.0000003861,
         location = "suburban Cook County",
         type = "municipality") %>% 
  filter(sqmi >= 4) %>% 
  select(-sqmi)

# create a novel geography in Cook County which combines both municipalities in suburban Cook County and communities areas in Chicago

novel_geo_cook <- places_cook_county %>% 
  bind_rows(community_areas) %>% 
  st_as_sf() %>% 
  st_make_valid()

```

## Merge select suburban Cook County and city of Chicago indicators

The next step is to download and merge similar indicator data from the two atlases for statistical analysis and mapping. Both suburban Cook County and the city of Chicago regularly survey their residents about health. Indicators derived from these surveys are shared on the atlases. Many indicators on the two atlases are aligned so that they can be compared across jurisdictions, including those below.

The following code downloads and combines a selection of health survey indicators that are comparable across both atlases. Below are links to each jurisdiction's charts and thematic maps for the selected indicators. Before running any statistics, review the indicators and form your own hypotheses about how they relate to one another and to active transportation: walking, bicycling, and public transit use.

-   Adult obesity rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8YZKL) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSOBP))
-   Neighborhood safety rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8SRFE) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSNSP))
-   Neighborhood sidewalk quality rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8IQGF) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSNSQP))
-   Neighborhood ambulatory difficulty rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/AMBDHSR) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSIDQZ))
-   Ease of walking to transit stop rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8OWII) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSWTSP))
-   Overall health status ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8OLNB) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSOHSP))
-   Physical inactivity rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8MIQE) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSPAP))

On **slide 1** of your presentation, speculate about the relationships between **two or more** of these indicators and how they may encourage or discourage active transportation. For each relationship you propose:

1.  **State the relationship and its expected direction.** For example, communities with higher physical inactivity rates may also report poorer overall health status, or places with better sidewalk quality may report easier walking access to transit stops.
2.  **Explain the mechanism.** Why might these indicators move together? Consider the built environment (sidewalks, transit access), perceptions (neighborhood safety), and individual capacity (ambulatory difficulty, obesity, overall health).
3.  **Connect it to walking, bicycling, and/or transit use.** For example, does feeling unsafe in a neighborhood discourage walking to a bus stop at night? Can poor sidewalks turn a short walk to transit into a barrier for someone with ambulatory difficulty?
4.  **Consider the direction of causality.** Does poor health lead to less walking and cycling, or does an environment that discourages active travel lead to poorer health? Could both be true, or could a third factor (e.g., income, car ownership, land use) explain both?
5.  **Anticipate geographic differences.** Would you expect these relationships to look the same in Chicago and suburban Cook County? Why or why not?

You will test these hypotheses with the merged data in the steps that follow, so treat this slide as a set of predictions that you will revisit.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

a_topic_list <- c("obesity", "safety", "sidewalk", "ambulatory", "transit", "health", "inactivity") # edit here
a_scc_topic_keys <- c("JG8YZKL","JG8SRFE","JG8IQGF","AMBDHSR","JG8OWII","JG8OLNB","JG8MIQE") # edit here
a_scc_topic_period <- c("2026","2026","2026","2026","2026","2026","2026") # edit here
a_chicago_topic_keys <- c("HCSOBP", "HCSNSP","HCSNSQP","HCSIDQZ","HCSWTSP","HCSOHSP","HCSPAP") # edit here
a_chicago_topic_period <- c("2023-2024","2023-2024","2023-2024","2022-2024","2023-2024","2023-2024","2023-2024") # edit here

# download SCC health survey indicators
for (i in 1:length(a_scc_topic_keys)){

  atopic_key <- a_scc_topic_keys[i]
  atopic_name <- a_topic_list[i]
  atopic_period <- a_scc_topic_period[i]
  
  #print(atopic_name)
  
  a_table_name <- paste0("scc_indicator_",atopic_name)

  a_topic_url <- paste0("https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/api/v1/data/?format=json&layer=place&period=",atopic_period,"&population=&topic=",atopic_key)
  
  a_topic_json <- fromJSON(a_topic_url)

  a_topic_df <- a_topic_json$results %>% 
    as.data.frame() %>% 
   select(estimate = v,
          se = se,
          geoid = g,
          layer = l) %>%
    mutate(topic = atopic_name)

  assign(a_table_name, a_topic_df)
  
}

# download Chicago health survey indicators
for (i in 1:length(a_chicago_topic_keys)){

  atopic_key <- a_chicago_topic_keys[i]
  atopic_name <- a_topic_list[i]
  atopic_period <- a_chicago_topic_period[i]
  
  #print(atopic_name)
  
  a_table_name <- paste0("chicago_indicator_",atopic_name)

  a_topic_url <- paste0("https://chicagohealthatlas.org/api/v1/data/?format=json&layer=neighborhood&period=",atopic_period,"&population=&topic=",atopic_key)
  
  a_topic_json <- fromJSON(a_topic_url)

  a_topic_df <- a_topic_json$results %>% 
    as.data.frame() %>% 
  select(estimate = v,
         se = se,
         geoid = g,
         layer = l) %>%
    mutate(topic = atopic_name,
           geoid= str_replace(geoid,"1714000-",""))

  assign(a_table_name, a_topic_df)
  
}

# bind SCC and Chicago indicators together
apattern <- "_indicator_"
alist_indicators <- mget(ls(pattern=apattern))
indicators_all <- rbindlist(alist_indicators)

# remove unneeded tables
rm(list=ls(pattern=apattern))

```

# Step #3 Map and explore indicators

## Join indicator attributes with county-wide geographies

Next, use the code below to join the indicator attributes to the county-wide geography layer. The result is a spatially enabled table that you will use to make custom maps in the steps that follow.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| eval: true
#| output: true

# reformat indicators in wide format
indicators_all_long <- indicators_all %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = "topic", values_from = c("estimate","se")) %>% 
  rename_with(~str_remove(., 'estimate_'))

# join indicator data with county-wide "novel" geography layer
indicators_all_long_geo <- novel_geo_cook %>% 
  left_join(indicators_all_long, by="geoid") %>% 
  st_as_sf() %>% 
  drop_na(layer)

```

## Create univariate maps of select indicators

Before measuring how indicators relate to one another, look at each indicator on its own. A univariate map shows one variable at a time and answers a simple question: *where* are rates high or low? It's easier to read correlations and bivariate maps once you know how each variable is distributed across the county.

@fig-communityarea_sccplaces is an interactive map of the new geography ("novel_geo_cook"). It combines suburban Cook County municipalities (dark gray border) and Chicago community areas (light gray border), with the merged indicators attached. Choose an indicator from the "Indicator" dropdown list in the upper right of the map to display it as a thematic map, grouped into quintiles (each about 20 percent of places); places without data for the selected indicator are shown in light gray. The city of Chicago boundary (dashed black line) and Cook County boundary (dark red line) make it easier to see where Chicago ends and suburban Cook County begins. Hover over or click individual places to see their values for every indicator.

Explore **at least two** of the indicators you discussed on slide 1. For each one, consider:

1.  **Overall pattern.** Are high and low rates clustered in certain parts of the county (e.g., the North Shore, the south suburbs, Chicago's South and West Sides, the downtown core)? Or are they scattered?
2.  **Extremes and outliers.** Which places have the highest and lowest rates? Do any places stand out sharply from their neighbors?
3.  **City–suburb boundary.** Do rates change abruptly at the Chicago city limits? If they do, think about whether that reflects real differences between places or differences in how the two jurisdictions run their surveys, word their questions, or estimate rates for small areas.
4.  **Missing or unreliable data.** Are any places blank or flagged? How might gaps affect what you conclude?
5.  **Comparison with your predictions.** Does the pattern match what you expected on slide 1? What surprised you, and what might explain it?

On **slides 2 and 3** of your presentation, paste one univariate map per slide, each showing a different indicator. Under each map, write 2–3 sentences that:

-   describe where rates are higher and lower,
-   point out at least one specific place or cluster that stands out, and
-   note whether the pattern supports, contradicts, or complicates the relationship you proposed on slide 1.

Then compare your two maps. Do high (or low) values of the two indicators seem to show up in the same places? Note your impressions. You'll test them formally with correlations and bivariate maps in the next step.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| label: fig-communityarea_sccplaces
#| fig-cap: Health Survey Indicators by Novel Cook County Geography (Quintiles)
#| warning: false

# display names for the indicators in the spatially enabled dataset (columns
# named in a_topic_list); indicators without a name here use their column name
indicator_names <- c(obesity = "Adult obesity rate",
                     safety = "Neighborhood safety rate",
                     sidewalk = "Neighborhood sidewalk quality rate",
                     ambulatory = "Ambulatory difficulty rate",
                     transit = "Ease of walking to transit stop rate",
                     health = "Overall health status rate",
                     inactivity = "Physical inactivity rate")
map_indicators <- intersect(a_topic_list, names(indicators_all_long_geo))
map_indicator_names <- ifelse(map_indicators %in% names(indicator_names),
                              indicator_names[map_indicators],
                              map_indicators)

# all county-wide geographies, with indicator values attached (places without
# data for an indicator are shown in grey)
map_data <- novel_geo_cook %>% 
  left_join(indicators_all_long_geo %>% 
              st_drop_geometry() %>% 
              select(geoid, all_of(map_indicators)),
            by = "geoid") %>% 
  st_transform(crs = 4326)

# borders: light grey for community areas and dark grey for municipalities
border_pal <- 
   colorFactor(palette = c("lightgrey", "darkgrey"), 
               levels = c("community area", "municipality"))

# hover (and click) labels with every indicator value
indicator_values <- sapply(seq_along(map_indicators), function(i) {
  x <- map_data[[map_indicators[i]]]
  sprintf("<i>%s:</i> %s<br/>", map_indicator_names[i],
          ifelse(is.na(x), "no data", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)))
})
indicator_values <- matrix(indicator_values, nrow = nrow(map_data))
novel_geography_labels <- paste0(
  "<strong>", map_data$name, "</strong><br/>",
  "<i>geoid:</i> ", map_data$geoid, "<br/>",
  "<i>type:</i> ", map_data$type, "<br/>",
  "<i>location:</i> ", map_data$location, "<hr style='margin: 3px 0;'/>",
  apply(indicator_values, 1, paste, collapse = ""))

# legend values (quintile ranges) to one decimal place
legend_format <- function(type, cuts, p) {
  values <- formatC(cuts, format = "f", digits = 1)
  paste0(values[-length(values)], " &ndash; ", values[-1])
}

# city of Chicago boundary (all community areas merged) and Cook County boundary
# (US Census Bureau cartographic boundary file, via tigris)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
chicago_boundary <- novel_geo_cook %>% 
  filter(type == "community area") %>% 
  st_union() %>% 
  st_sf(name = "City of Chicago", geometry = .) %>% 
  st_transform(crs = 4326)
cook_county_boundary <- counties(state = "IL", cb = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE) %>% 
  filter(NAME == "Cook") %>% 
  st_transform(crs = 4326)

# interactive map
indicator_map <-
leaflet() %>% 
  addTiles(urlTemplate = paste0(
      "https://basemaps.cartocdn.com/rastertiles/light_all/{z}/{x}/{y}.png?key=",
      "cb1_31xh_1_06fb99adb466f0f5a0392d7d")) %>% 
  addResetMapButton() %>%
    addFullscreenControl() %>%
  # addProviderTiles(
  #   "CartoDB.Positron",
  #   group = "CartoDB.Positron") %>% 
  addPolygons(
    data = map_data,
    label = lapply(novel_geography_labels, htmltools::HTML),
    popup = novel_geography_labels,
    weight = 1,
    opacity = 1,
    fillColor = "white",
    color = border_pal(map_data$type),
    fillOpacity = 0.2,
    group = "None (geography only)"
    ) %>% 
  addLegend("bottomright",
            colors = c("lightgrey", "darkgrey", "#000000", "#7a0019"),
            labels = c("Community area (Chicago)", "Municipality (suburban Cook County)",
                       "City of Chicago boundary", "Cook County boundary"),
            title = "Boundaries",
            opacity = 1)

# one layer (and legend) per indicator, grouped into quintiles
for (i in seq_along(map_indicators)) {
  values <- map_data[[map_indicators[i]]]
  if (all(is.na(values))) next # skip indicators without any data
  breaks <- unique(quantile(values, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2), na.rm = TRUE))
  indicator_pal <- colorBin(palette = "YlGnBu", domain = values, bins = breaks, na.color = "#e0e0e0")
  indicator_map <- indicator_map %>% 
    addPolygons(
      data = map_data,
      label = lapply(novel_geography_labels, htmltools::HTML),
      popup = novel_geography_labels,
      weight = 1,
      opacity = 1,
      fillColor = indicator_pal(values),
      color = border_pal(map_data$type),
      fillOpacity = 0.7,
      group = map_indicator_names[i]) %>% 
    addLegend("bottomleft",
              pal = indicator_pal,
              values = values,
              title = paste0(map_indicator_names[i], "<br/>(quintiles)"),
              labFormat = legend_format,
              opacity = 0.7,
              className = paste0("info legend indicator-legend indicator-legend-", i))
}

# city of Chicago and Cook County boundaries, drawn above the indicator layers
# in their own pane; they do not respond to the mouse, so the hover labels of
# the places beneath them still work
indicator_map <- indicator_map %>% 
  addMapPane("boundaries", zIndex = 450) %>% 
  addPolygons(
    data = cook_county_boundary,
    fill = FALSE,
    color = "#7a0019",
    weight = 3,
    opacity = 0.9,
    options = pathOptions(pane = "boundaries", interactive = FALSE)) %>% 
  addPolygons(
    data = chicago_boundary,
    fill = FALSE,
    color = "#000000",
    weight = 2.5,
    opacity = 0.9,
    dashArray = "6 4",
    options = pathOptions(pane = "boundaries", interactive = FALSE))

# dropdown list (top right) that shows one indicator layer and legend at a time;
# the first indicator is shown when the map opens (choose "None" to show
# only the geography)
indicator_map %>% 
  htmlwidgets::onRender("
    function(el, x, data) {
      var map = this;
      var groups = [].concat(data.groups);
      function show(i) {
        groups.forEach(function(g, j) {
          var layer = map.layerManager.getLayerGroup(g, false);
          if (layer) { if (j === i) { map.addLayer(layer); } else { map.removeLayer(layer); } }
        });
        el.querySelectorAll('.indicator-legend').forEach(function(d) {
          d.style.display = d.classList.contains('indicator-legend-' + i) ? '' : 'none';
        });
      }
      var control = L.control({position: 'topright'});
      control.onAdd = function() {
        var div = L.DomUtil.create('div', 'leaflet-bar');
        div.style.background = 'white';
        div.style.padding = '4px 6px';
        div.innerHTML = '<label style=\"font-weight: bold; margin-right: 4px;\">Indicator</label>';
        var select = L.DomUtil.create('select', '', div);
        groups.forEach(function(g, j) {
          var option = L.DomUtil.create('option', '', select);
          option.value = j;
          option.text = g;
        });
        select.value = groups.length > 1 ? 1 : 0;
        select.onchange = function() { show(parseInt(select.value)); };
        L.DomEvent.disableClickPropagation(div);
        L.DomEvent.disableScrollPropagation(div);
        return div;
      };
      control.addTo(map);
      show(groups.length > 1 ? 1 : 0);
    }", data = list(groups = c("None (geography only)", map_indicator_names)))

```

# Step 4. Examine statistical relationships between selected variables

Use the code below to create a bivariate correlation plot to explore the statistical relationships between the seven downloaded indicator variables. Pearson's bivariate correlation (or Pearson's r) quantifies the strength and direction of the linear relationship between each pair of variables. The coefficients ranges from -1 to +1 with values greater than 0 indicating positive linear relationships (i.e., as one variable increases, the other variable also increases) and values less than 0 indicating a negative linear relationship (i.e., as one variable decreases, the other variable also decreases). @fig-correlation_plots shows two plots based on the same correlation matrix: Plot 1 shows explicit correlation statistics and plot 2 shows graduated circles.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-bivariate_correlation_plots

# subset indicator data for statistical analysis
indicators_all_long_sub <- indicators_all_long_geo %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  drop_na() %>% 
  select(-starts_with("se"), -c(geoid,name,type, location,layer))
  
# calculate bivariate correlations between all numeric variables
variable_biv_correlations <- cor(indicators_all_long_sub, method="pearson")

# create correlation plot option 1 with correlation values
corrplot_1 <- corrplot(variable_biv_correlations, method="number", col=c("black","white"), order="hclust", bg="lightgrey", tl.col = "grey")

# create correlation plot option 2 with graduated circles
corrplot_2 <- corrplot(variable_biv_correlations, col=c("black","white"), order="hclust", bg="lightgrey", tl.col = "grey")

# display correlation plot option 1
corrplot_1

# display correlation plot option 2
corrplot_2
```

# Step 5. Create two custom bivariate maps

Adapt the code below (i.e.., look for the "edit here" comments) to create two custom single variable (univariate) and bivariate thematic / choropleth maps similar to those displayed in @fig-univariate_maps and @fig-bivariate_map. The univariate maps are categorized into quintiles from quintile 1 (representing the lowest performing areas) to quintile 5 (the highest performing areas). Each quintile represents about 20 percent of the geographies mapped (i.e., about 40). *Add your custom maps to slides 2-4 of your presentation and describe the spatial patterns you see in each map.*

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| output: true

# Create two bivariate thematic/choropleth maps 
# modify variable(s) to be mapped and legend names/titles for all maps

# bivariate map 1 legend
map1.legend <- bi_legend(pal = "BlueGold",
                    dim = 3,
                    xlab = "Health", # edit here
                    ylab = "Access", # edit here
                    size = 8,
                    pad_width = 1)

map1.bivariate <- ggdraw() +
  draw_plot(map1, 0, 0, 1, 1) +
  draw_plot(map1.legend, 0.2, 0.45, 0.35, 0.2)

# display bivariate map
map1.bivariate

# bivariate map 2 legend
map2.legend <- bi_legend(pal = "BlueGold",
                    dim = 3,
                    xlab = "Health", # edit here
                    ylab = "Access", # edit here
                    size = 8,
                    pad_width = 1)

map2.bivariate <- ggdraw() +
  draw_plot(map1, 0, 0, 1, 1) +
  draw_plot(map1.legend, 0.2, 0.45, 0.35, 0.2)

# display bivariate map 2
map2.bivariate
```
